posts.title: The red miso fire gets redder
posts.excerpt: A second chili paste, toasted miso and corn until the end of October: what changed in our loudest bowl, and why.
posts.content:
The red miso fire started as a slow-Tuesday experiment and became the second-best-selling button on the machine. This month it changes for the first time.

Two chili pastes

The old bowl used one roasted chili paste. The new one adds a fermented paste with garlic and a little sugar, so the heat arrives in two waves: first the bright one, then the deep one.

Toasted miso

Yui now toasts the red miso in the wok with lard before it meets the broth. It takes four extra minutes per batch and makes the soup taste like it has been on the fire twice as long.

  • Two chili pastes instead of one
  • Miso toasted in the wok first
  • Sweet corn until the end of October
  • Same price on the machine

If it is still not hot enough, the chili bomb ticket is right next to it.

posts.title: How the ticket machine works (and why we keep it)
posts.excerpt: Coins, notes, IC cards and the one button everyone misses. A first-timer’s guide to the machine by the door.
posts.content:
Every week someone walks in, sits down and waits for a menu. There is no menu at the counter: there is a machine by the door. Here is how it works.

  1. Put in coins, notes or tap an IC card
  2. Push the button for your bowl: it lights up when you have paid enough
  3. Push more buttons for toppings, sides and drinks
  4. Take the tickets and the change, then sit down

Why a machine?

Nobody handles money at the counter, so the cooks never stop cooking. The line moves faster, and you can take as long as you like choosing without anyone watching.

The button everyone misses

Kaedama, the extra noodles, is at the bottom right. Buy it later, when your noodles are gone and you still have soup.

posts.title: Eighteen hours of broth, hour by hour
posts.excerpt: From six in the morning to midnight: what goes into the pot, when, and why the fire never goes out.
posts.content:
The tonkotsu pot is the first thing Kenta touches in the morning and the last thing anyone looks at before closing.

06:00 · Bones in

Pork bones, blanched and scrubbed, go into cold water with chicken frames. The fire goes to full.

12:00 · The white turns

After six hours of a hard boil the fat and collagen start to emulsify and the broth turns white. We top it up with water every hour.

18:00 · Fish and kombu

A separate pot of kombu and dried sardines is made for the shoyu and blended into a little of the tonkotsu for the evening.

00:00 · Strain

What is left is strained and cooled. Some of it starts tomorrow’s pot. That is why it never tastes quite the same twice.

posts.title: Four noodles, cut every morning
posts.excerpt: Thin, straight, wavy and thick: which noodle goes into which bowl, and why Yui makes them all before nine.
posts.content:
Yui starts mixing flour at seven. By nine there are four kinds of noodles resting in the fridge.

  • Thin and straight for tonkotsu and shio yuzu
  • Medium and straight for shoyu
  • Wavy for the red miso fire: the curls hold the soup
  • Thick for tsukemen, served cold

Every noodle uses the same flour; only the water, the thickness and the rest time change. Firmness is your call: tell us when you hand over your ticket.

posts.title: The gyoza lace skirt, explained
posts.excerpt: Flour, water and a hot pan: how six dumplings end up joined by a crisp golden lace, and the right way to break it.
posts.content:
Gyoza arrive upside down on the plate, joined by a thin golden crust. That is the hanetsuki, the “wings”, and it is the best part.

How it is made

The gyoza fry in a little oil, then a slurry of flour and water goes into the pan. The water steams the dumplings; the flour stays behind and crisps into lace.

How to eat it

Break off one dumpling with its piece of lace, dip it in vinegar, soy and chili oil, and eat it in one bite while it is hot.

posts.title: Open late: the new night hours
posts.excerpt: From August the counter stays open until two in the morning, Tuesday to Saturday. Here is what changes at night.
posts.content:
From August the counter stays open until two in the morning from Tuesday to Saturday. Lunch stays the same.

At night the machine gets two extra buttons: a half-size tonkotsu for the last bowl of the evening, and a cold beer with gyoza set. The current hours are always on the Map page and at the bottom of every page.

Please keep it quiet in the alley after midnight. Our neighbours sleep upstairs.
